strengths: The paper presents a complete, coherent framework for low-rank variational inference in BNNs, implemented from scratch for MLPs, LSTMs, and Transformers, with architecture-specific care (e.g., cached weight sampling for LSTMs per Fortunato et al., position-wise factorization for Transformers).

The Gaussian complexity transfer result (Section 3.5 / Appendix E) is the strongest technical contribution: the observation that the posterior predictive mean lies in the closed convex hull of the rank-r support class, combined with convex-hull and closure invariance of vector-valued Gaussian complexity, cleanly extends deterministic rank-sensitive bounds (Pinto et al., 2025) to Bayesian predictors. This is a genuinely nice, self-contained argument.

Empirical evaluation is broad (MIMIC-III, Beijing air quality, SST-2, MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, toy regression) with a consistent narrative of a calibration-OOD tradeoff, selective prediction gains, and parameter efficiency (up to 15x fewer parameters than Deep Ensembles).

The limitations discussion is unusually honest: the authors acknowledge that Gaussian complexity bounds are vacuous in practice, that training-time gains do not materialize at small scales, that confidence intervals overlap across seeds, and that comparisons with SWAG and low-rank covariance methods are missing.

Reproducibility is well supported: detailed hardware/software configuration, seeds, hyperparameter choices, KL annealing schedules, and rank-selection procedures are documented in Appendices F, G, and H.
weaknesses: The central 'singularity' claim (Theorem 3.4) is over-sold. That the pushforward of a distribution through W = AB^T is singular w.r.t. Lebesgue measure is an immediate consequence of any low-rank parameterization (including LoRA, rank-1 perturbations, subspace inference) and requires only standard measure theory. It does not distinguish this method from other low-rank approaches as strongly as the framing suggests.

The PAC-Bayes result (Theorem 3.8) is essentially a parameter-counting argument relying on the assumption of equal per-parameter KL bounds; the interesting question of whether the actual KL for low-rank posteriors is genuinely smaller is not established. The Gaussian complexity bounds are admittedly vacuous, so the theoretical 'provable benefits' claimed in the abstract are not supported by non-vacuous guarantees.

Theorems 3.6/3.7 compare a learned W to an unknown full-rank optimum W*; the decomposition into learning error ||W - W*_r||_F and rank bias is informative only if the full-rank optimum has fast singular value decay, which is validated only empirically on a handful of layers. The bounds are thus loose and somewhat circular as guidance.

Originality relative to prior Bayesian low-rank methods (Bayesian-LoRA of Yang et al. 2024, BLoB, BELLA, subspace inference, low-rank covariance VI) is incremental; the main differentiator is training from random initialization rather than any new variational family. The claim that 'no prior work trains low-rank BNNs end-to-end' is asserted but not rigorously substantiated.

Experimental scale is modest relative to the scalability claims: the largest model is a 9.9M-parameter BERT-mini-style transformer trained from scratch (SST-2 accuracy ~0.80, well below pre-trained-model baselines), and there is no comparison with SGLD, SWAG, or low-rank covariance methods (acknowledged). With only 4-5 seeds and overlapping intervals, several headline improvements (e.g., OOD detection over Deep Ensembles on MIMIC-III) are not statistically established.

Some presentation and consistency issues: Table 2 contains missing/placeholder entries for the deterministic baseline; numbers in the appendix occasionally differ from the main text (e.g., AUPR-OOD 0.81 in Figure 11 vs 0.788 in Table 1); the seeding of figures vs tables (5 seeds vs 4 runs) is inconsistent in places.

The initialization theory in Appendix F matches only second moments of the posterior mean of W and glosses over the fact that induced weight entries are correlated with each other and that sampling noise contributes additional variance, weakening the claimed 'principled' foundation.

strengths: The paper is thorough in execution: it implements the low-rank variational layer from scratch for three architecture families (MLPs, LSTMs, Transformers) with architecture-specific handling (cached weight sampling for LSTMs following Fortunato et al., token-batch sparsity for embeddings), and evaluates on four distinct tasks (MIMIC-III, Beijing PM2.5, SST-2, plus MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/toy regression in the appendix) with multiple baselines and 4–5 seeds each.

Reproducibility is strong: complete hyperparameters, hardware/software versions, seed handling, KL annealing schedules, rank-selection procedures, and model specification tables (Tables 6–8) are provided in Appendix G.

The limitations discussion is candid and does not oversell: the authors explicitly acknowledge overlapping confidence intervals, the calibration gap relative to Deep Ensembles, the lack of wall-clock speedup at small scale (Table 9 shows low-rank is actually slower than Full-Rank BBB), the fact that Gaussian complexity bounds are vacuous (Figure 3), and that SVD initialization shows no consistent benefit.

The observation that parameter reduction does not uniformly translate to training speedups at small scale, and the analysis of why (kernel launch overhead, dual sampling), is a useful practical insight; the SST-2 scaling result (8.2 vs 23.1 minutes) is a genuine demonstration of benefit at larger scale.

The convex-hull/closure invariance argument in Appendix E (Lemmas E.9–E.11, Proposition E.13) transferring deterministic rank-sensitive Gaussian complexity bounds of Pinto et al. (2025) to the Bayesian predictive mean is a clean, correct, and somewhat novel technical observation, including the thoughtful treatment of high-probability vs almost-sure spectral norm bounds (Section E.10).
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and the central claim of end-to-end low-rank BNNs is overstated. The parameterization W = AB^T with factorized Gaussian posteriors is a very direct combination of Bayes-by-Backprop with LoRA-style factorization; the paper itself cites low-rank covariance VI (Tomczak et al., 2020; Swiatkowski et al., 2020), Bayesian LoRA variants (Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Doan et al., 2025), and rank-1 perturbations (Dusenberry et al., 2020a). The distinction reduces to 'the mean is also low-rank,' which is a modest delta, and comparisons against these most-similar methods (e.g., BLoB) are missing from the experiments; the authors concede this in the limitations.

The headline theoretical results are largely trivial repackaged as significant contributions. Theorem 3.4 (singularity of the induced posterior) follows immediately from rank(W) ≤ r and standard measure-zero arguments — the authors' own Appendix B.6 admits it is 'not a computational obstacle' and the manuscript sells it as a key geometric novelty. Theorem 3.8 (PAC-Bayes) is essentially parameter counting under a crude McAllester bound with an assumed-equal per-parameter KL, and the 'tighter bounds' conclusion is vacuous in practice as Figure 3 itself shows. Theorem 3.6/3.7 concern approximating the optimal single-layer weight by truncated SVD — a deterministic linear-algebra exercise that does not address the Bayesian posterior or deep-network composition; the Bayesian extension (Theorem C.8) is loose and not connected back to the method.

Empirical support for the central claims is mixed. The low-rank model is consistently worse than Deep Ensembles on NLL/ECE (the calibration metrics it is supposed to improve), and on SST-2 the deterministic baseline (0.812 accuracy, 0.490 NLL) outperforms all Bayesian methods including low-rank (0.806, 0.527). The claimed improvement is mainly on OOD detection metrics, where the authors themselves acknowledge overlapping confidence intervals across seeds, and the low-rank method is slower in wall-clock time at two of the three main scales (Tables 9, 12).

Internal inconsistencies and presentation issues undermine confidence: Figure 10's discussion states the selected MIMIC-III rank configuration achieves AUROC ≈ 0.72 while Table 1 reports 0.802 for Low-Rank and Figure 11 reports AUPR-OOD of 0.81 vs 0.788 in Table 1; Figure 5's caption claims Deep Ensemble 'achieves best point predictions at 100% retention' yet Table 11 shows Deep Ensemble at 10.40 and Full-Rank BBB at 10.66; the heavy use of radar plots (Figures 4, 6, 8, 12, 17) duplicates table content without adding information; typos persist ('Thi approach' in A.4, 'an Appendix I' in Section 2, mismatched notation such as lr vs r in Theorem 3.7).

The method's 'principled' framing is weakened by heavy per-task tuning: the KL weight β spans three orders of magnitude across experiments (0.001/Nbatches to 0.5/Nbatches), rank is selected per layer via ablation, and damping constants are dataset-specific (Table 6), so the reported advantages may partly reflect tuning budget rather than the factorization itself. The rank-selection procedure is also confounded: ablation selects the best configuration on validation OOD metrics, which is exactly the quantity being claimed as the method's advantage.

The ECE comparison protocol (selecting the best of 6 binning configurations per model) is nonstandard and could bias cross-model comparisons, even though the appendix's robustness checks partly mitigate this concern.

strengths: The paper develops a complete, end-to-end low-rank variational inference framework for BNNs with drop-in variational layers for three architecture families (MLPs, LSTMs, Transformers), implemented from scratch with careful architecture-specific handling (tied LSTM weights, batch-sparse embedding sampling, cached weight sampling per Fortunato et al.).

The theoretical treatment is thorough and well-organized: the singularity of the induced posterior (Thm 3.4), structured covariance characterization (Lemma 3.5), an EYM-based decomposition of approximation error into learning error and rank bias (Thm 3.6/3.7), PAC-Bayes bounds scaling as r(m+n), and a genuinely neat Gaussian-complexity transfer argument (Prop E.13) showing the posterior-mean predictor lies in the closed convex hull of the rank-r class, whose complexity is invariant under convex hull/closure. The proofs in Appendices B-E are complete and largely correct.

The empirical evaluation is broad (MIMIC-III, Beijing PM2.5, SST-2, MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, toy regression) with multiple baselines (deterministic, Deep Ensemble, Full-Rank BBB, Rank-1 multiplicative, SVD init), multi-seed runs with reported standard deviations, extensive hyperparameter analysis (KL annealing, rank ablations, Pareto frontier plots), and honest reporting of negative findings (SVD init gives no consistent benefit; overlapping confidence intervals; vacuous PAC-Bayes/Gaussian-complexity bounds).

The limitations discussion is candid and specific: the calibration gap relative to Deep Ensembles, tuning burden of β and r, absence of wall-clock speedups at small scale (with a sensible GPU-overhead explanation), and the need for broader baselines (SWAG, low-rank covariance methods).

Useful practical side contributions: principled variance-matching initialization for low-rank factors (Appendix F), and an analysis of when to prefer rank vs. calibration metrics in deployment (selective prediction results in Table 11).
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work. The core method — mean-field Gaussian posteriors over factors A, B with W = AB^T — is very close to Bella (Doan et al., 2025), Bayesian LoRA variants (Yang et al., 2024; BLoB), and low-rank covariance methods (Tomczak et al., 2020; Swiatkowski et al., 2020). The claimed differentiators (end-to-end from random init, no pretrained backbone) narrow the delta considerably, and Table 4's positioning does not quantify any performance advantage over these closest baselines, none of which are actually run in the experiments.

The headline theoretical results are assembled from standard ingredients. Theorem 3.4 (singularity) is an immediate consequence of pushforward support plus measure-zero of the rank manifold; Theorems 3.6/3.7 apply EYM plus a Lipschitz argument to the deterministic (not Bayesian) setting, with the Bayesian extension relegated to a remark. Theorem 3.8's 'tighter PAC-Bayes bound' assumes equal per-parameter KL divergences (Cmax^full = Cmax^LR), an assumption that is asserted, not verified empirically; the complexity ratio in Eq. (5) is a heuristic comparison of upper bounds.

The generalization bounds are admitted to be practically vacuous: Figure 3 shows the PAC-Bayes bound crosses the vacuity threshold at r* ≈ 11 and Gaussian complexity bounds are vacuous for both methods, so the theory provides 'insight' rather than the practical guarantees claimed in the introduction.

The Gaussian-complexity transfer (Thm 3.9) requires almost-sure spectral norm bounds (Assumption E.4), which Gaussian posteriors violate; the high-probability fixes in E.10 require convex losses and add a δtotal term with the empirical loss computed on the rejection-sampled f_good predictor rather than the deployed model — a practically awkward bound not evaluated empirically.

Empirical results are mixed on modest scales. Low-rank consistently loses to Deep Ensembles on NLL/ECE and often to Full-Rank BBB on calibration; headline gains are in OOD metrics, some with overlapping confidence intervals (acknowledged). Full-Rank BBB's OOD AUROC of 0.492 on Beijing (below the deterministic 0.5 baseline) and the blank/typo cells in Table 2 suggest presentation or experimental issues. Architectures are small (2-layer MLP hidden 128; 2-layer LSTM hidden 64; 4-layer 256-dim Transformer), so the scalability narrative remains speculative.

No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility given the from-scratch TensorFlow implementation and many architecture-specific choices (damping constants like '0.32 for r ≤ 5, 0.55 for r > 5' are underexplained).

Inconsistencies undermine polish: Table 1 lists deterministic params 22.4K vs. 20.5K in Table 6; Beijing test size differs between main text (6,260) and Appendix G.4 (7,553); Table 2's Deterministic row contains empty cells and malformed entries; text reports '5-member Deep Ensemble' advantages in the abstract while 1-vs-5 comparisons conflate per-model and total costs (per-model comparisons are left to future work).

strengths: The paper is technically solid and self-contained: all main theorems (singularity of the induced posterior, EYM-based loss decomposition, PAC-Bayes parameter-count comparison, and the Gaussian-complexity transfer to posterior predictive means) come with complete appendix proofs that I found essentially correct, including the neat convex-hull/closure invariance argument (Lemmas E.9–E.11) showing rank-sensitive complexity bounds transfer to the BNN predictive mean despite rank destruction under expectation.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough and honest: four task families (MLP/tabular, LSTM/time-series, Transformer/NLP, plus MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/toy regression), 4–5 seeds with mean ± std, rank ablations with Pareto-frontier analysis, a controlled matched profiling benchmark, sensitivity of ECE to binning schemes, MI vs STD uncertainty comparisons, multi-seed SWAG comparisons, and an honest treatment of the calibration–OOD tradeoff (e.g., Deep Ensembles remain stronger on NLL/in-domain AUROC on MIMIC-III and SST-2, and the paper says so).

Reproducibility is strong: full hardware/software configuration, deterministic operations, exact seeds, KL annealing schedules, initialization recipes (Section F), and a controlled profiling protocol are all documented.

The limitations discussion is candid and does not overstate: it acknowledges overlapping confidence intervals, the need for rank/KL tuning, the calibration gap relative to ensembles, and that parameter reduction translates mainly to memory (not wall-clock) savings at small scale.
The comparison with adjacent literatures (Appendix A, Table 5) is careful and positions the end-to-end-from-initialization setting against post-hoc and covariance-based low-rank methods.
weaknesses: Originality is modest. The core method — mean-field Gaussian posteriors on factors A, B of W = AB^T — is a natural combination of known ingredients (Bayesian matrix factorization, low-rank covariance VI, subspace inference, probabilistic LoRA variants such as BLoB/Bayesian-LoRA/Bella). The headline 'singularity' result (Theorem 3.4) is mathematically elementary: pushforward of any distribution on the factors onto the rank-r manifold is singular w.r.t. Lebesgue measure because that manifold has measure zero — a well-known fact in the subspace-inference literature. The title and framing (including 'measure-theoretic singularity' as a distinguishing feature) oversell a straightforward observation, and the paper does not engage with the deeper consequences of singular posteriors (e.g., prior/posterior geometry, KL mis-specification between factor and weight spaces) that Watanabe-style singularity theory actually addresses (only via a disclaimer footnote).

The theoretical results are largely incremental and rest on questionable assumptions. The PAC-Bayes complexity-ratio 'theorem' (3.8) is essentially parameter counting under the assumption C_max^full = C_max^LR, which is unlikely to hold in practice since per-parameter KLs differ between parameterizations; the KL bound itself (Lemma D.3, max per-coordinate KL × dimension) is crude. The EYM-based loss bounds (Theorems 3.6–3.7) are stated for a single-layer linear model applied per weight matrix; extension to deep networks (composition of Lipschitz layers) is not carried through, so the connection between the theory and the actual MLP/LSTM/Transformer experiments is loose. The Gaussian-complexity theorem is essentially a transfer of Pinto et al. (2025) plus the standard convex-hull invariance of Gaussian complexity.

There is a theory–practice gap the paper does not fully resolve: the loss approximation analysis treats learned weights as fixed points and does not connect the variational posterior, KL term, or β-scaling to the bounds; conversely, the bounds are never empirically validated as informative certificates (the paper itself concedes both PAC-Bayes and Gaussian complexity bounds are vacuous, Figure 3).

Empirical gains are mixed and modest in magnitude: on MIMIC-III, low-rank is clearly worse than Deep Ensembles and the deterministic baseline in-domain (AUROC 0.895 vs 0.929/0.922, NLL 0.433 vs 0.300); on SST-2, Deep Ensembles beat it on accuracy, NLL, and OOD AUROC. The strongest selling points (AUPR-Err, AUPR-In, PICP, selective prediction) are secondary reliability metrics, some confidence intervals overlap across seeds, and statistical significance is not established. At transformer scale the in-domain accuracy still trails the deterministic baseline (0.806 vs 0.812) despite heavy parameterization tuning (r=16, embedding sparsity tricks, damped initialization), raising questions about whether the factorization is a net win versus simpler alternatives.

The supplementary low-rank ensembling study (Appendix H.5), which is used to argue the calibration gap is mitigable, is based on a single ensemble run — and ironically shows that the efficiency argument then collapses (5 low-rank members ≈ Deep Ensemble cost).

Presentation issues: many figures (radar plots, ablation scatter plots, some heatmaps) are cluttered and hard to read; the main text is dense with appendix forward-references; some minor inconsistencies (e.g., SWAG's 208.37M parameters vs the 9.9M backbone in Table 9 suggests the SWAG configuration differs materially from the compared models, which weakens that comparison).

strengths: Extensive and fairly thorough empirical evaluation: the paper tests the proposed low-rank variational BNN across MLPs, LSTMs, and Transformers on four benchmark settings (MIMIC-III, Beijing PM2.5, SST-2, plus MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/toy regression in the appendix), against a reasonably broad set of baselines (deterministic, Deep Ensembles, full-rank BBB, Rank-1 multiplicative, LR-SVD init, and supplementary multi-seed SWAG comparisons).

Good experimental hygiene: 4-5 random seeds per experiment with reported standard deviations, a controlled matched profiling benchmark (Table 4, Appendix G.5.4/H.4.1) to separate parameter savings from wall-clock speedups, and a careful discussion of when low-rank helps (Transformer scale) versus where it does not (MIMIC-III training time, Table 10).

Honest limitations discussion: the paper openly acknowledges overlapping confidence intervals, the calibration gap relative to Deep Ensembles, the need for rank/KL tuning, and that some gains (e.g., SST-2 low-rank ensemble in H.5) rest on a single run. It also does not overstate results against Deep Ensembles.

Strong reproducibility: complete hardware/software details, seeds, preprocessing pipelines, and implementation protocol for each dataset; the implementation is described at a level of detail that would allow replication.

Complete proof appendices: all stated lemmas/theorems are proven, and potentially contentious assumptions (almost-sure spectral norm bounds, high-probability relaxations in E.10) are addressed with explicit alternatives.
weaknesses: The central theoretical contribution is much thinner than advertised. Theorem 3.4 (singularity of the induced posterior) is an immediate consequence of the pushforward of any distribution over factors onto the rank-r manifold having measure-zero support; the paper itself concedes this is unrelated to singular learning theory (footnote 1), making the title and framing of the paper somewhat misleading. Lemma 3.5 is a routine covariance computation. The Eckart-Young-Mirsky-based Theorems 3.6-3.7 are direct compositions of Lipschitz continuity with the classical EYM theorem.

The loss-approximation guarantees apply only to a single linear layer with one weight matrix, not to deep nonlinear networks: Theorems 3.6-3.7 bound |ℓ(Wx,y) − ℓ(W*x,y)| for a single matrix W acting on x. In an actual deep network, per-layer rank truncation does not translate into a bound on network loss because of nonlinear composition across layers. Framing this as a theory of 'Singular Bayesian Neural Networks' significantly overreaches.

The PAC-Bayes result (Theorem 3.8) is a heuristic parameter-counting argument, not a genuine tighter bound. The claimed superiority of the low-rank complexity term requires assuming equal per-parameter KL (Cmax^full = Cmax^LR, Appendix D.3), which is not verified; the factors' KL to the prior could be larger, and the comparison is between two different posteriors with different empirical risks. The empirical PAC-Bayes and Gaussian complexity bounds in Figure 3 are admitted by the authors to be vacuous, so the theory has no demonstrated practical consequence.

The Gaussian complexity transfer result (Section 3.5, Appendix E) relies on Assumption E.4 (almost-sure spectral norm bounds on factors), which Gaussian posteriors—the ones actually used in all experiments—violate. The high-probability fix (Appendix E.10) additionally requires convexity of the loss and introduces a slack term δ_total, and the resulting bounds are acknowledged to be vacuous. The core observation (Gaussian complexity invariance under convex hull and closure, Lemmas E.9-E.10) is standard functional analysis.

Novelty is modest relative to the positioning claim that 'no prior work trains low-rank BNNs end-to-end... with rigorous theoretical guarantees.' End-to-end low-rank/Bayesian-LoRA methods (Doan et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024; Meo et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024) are closely related; the paper's Appendix A differentiation is largely about end-to-end vs. pretrained backbones and support geometry, and the differentiating theory is itself weak (see above).

Empirical results are mixed and the headline metric is questionable: the 'up to 33× fewer parameters than 5-member Deep Ensembles' claim compares a single model against the summed parameters of five members, which is an unfair accounting for any single-model method. On in-distribution metrics the method generally does not beat Deep Ensembles, and calibration is often worse (e.g., NLL 0.433 vs 0.300 on MIMIC-III; NLL 0.527 vs 0.434 on SST-2). The OOD advantage is task-dependent (strong on MIMIC-III, weaker on SST-2 where Deep Ensembles win on both NLL and AUROC-OOD).

The practical efficiency story is weaker than the abstract suggests: at small/medium scale, low-rank methods are actually slower than full-rank BBB despite 70% fewer parameters (Table 10), and the efficiency gains materialize only for the larger Transformer—while the claimed scaling to 'larger language models' remains future work.

The posterior formulation has structural concerns that are not deeply analyzed: the scale non-identifiability of W = AB^T is only addressed at initialization (Appendix F.5), and the induced posterior's mean is a rank-r matrix by construction, but the consequences for posterior expressiveness versus bias in deep, multi-layer settings are not systematically studied beyond a hypothesis in Section 4.6.

strengths: Comprehensive and carefully executed empirical study: three architecture families (MLP, LSTM, Transformer) across four benchmark settings (MIMIC-III, Beijing PM2.5, SST-2, plus MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/toy in the appendix), with multiple baselines (deterministic, Deep Ensemble, Full-Rank BBB, Rank-1 multiplicative, SWAG), many uncertainty metrics, and multi-seed runs with mean±std reporting.

The Gaussian complexity transfer (Appendix E) is a genuinely nice technical observation: posterior-mean predictors belong to the closed convex hull of the support class, and vector-valued Gaussian complexity is invariant under convex hull and closure, so deterministic rank-sensitive bounds (Pinto et al., 2025) transfer to Bayesian predictive means without degradation. The high-probability relaxation (Section E.10) is handled carefully, including the necessity of loss convexity.

Honest and thorough limitations discussion: the calibration–OOD tradeoff is described as task-dependent rather than uniform; overlapping confidence intervals are acknowledged; supplementary low-rank ensembling is offered as a mitigation; SWAG comparisons are included and reported even where SWAG wins (e.g., MIMIC-III AUROC/NLL).

Strong reproducibility support: detailed hardware/software configuration, deterministic TF operations, seed policies, rank-ablation protocols, a controlled matched profiling benchmark to separate pipeline effects from method effects, and a rank-sweep profiling study clarifying that runtime gains are sublinear in parameter reduction.
The loss approximation decomposition (learning error vs. rank bias via EYM) connects theory to a practical decision (rank selection) and is validated empirically via singular value decay analysis.
weaknesses: Originality is limited and the novelty claim is overstated. Low-rank variational posteriors for BNNs are well explored (Tomczak et al. 2020, Swiatkowski et al. 2020, Bella/Doan et al. 2025, Bayesian-LoRA variants Yang et al. 2024, BLoB/Wang et al. 2024). The claimed delta — end-to-end from random initialization plus theory — is real but narrow, and the paper does not empirically compare against any of these closest methods (Section 5 admits broader comparisons with low-rank covariance methods would strengthen positioning).

The headline 'singularity' framing is largely rhetorical. Theorem 3.4 (pushforward of a factorized posterior is supported on the rank-r manifold, which has Lebesgue measure zero) is a textbook observation dressed in measure-theoretic language; Theorem 3.8's intuition, Lemma 3.5's covariance structure, and Figure 2 do not establish consequences that go beyond the obvious fact that the parameterization constrains the support.

The 'provably tighter generalization bounds' claim (Theorem 3.8) is questionable. It compares PAC-Bayes complexity terms of two different posterior families under an equal per-parameter KL assumption (Cmax^full = Cmax^LR) that need not hold — the priors on factors induce a different prior on W than a mean-field prior on W, so the KL terms are not directly commensurable. Moreover, the two bounds attach to different posteriors with different empirical risks, so a smaller complexity ratio for Q_LR does not by itself yield a tighter bound for the low-rank model relative to a single baseline.

The Gaussian complexity bounds are acknowledged to be vacuous in practice (Figure 3, Section 3.5), and the reported PAC-Bayes bound only becomes non-vacuous at very low ranks (r*≈11), limiting the practical value of the generalization theory.

Empirical results are mixed relative to the strongest baseline: Deep Ensembles remain better on in-distribution AUROC/NLL on MIMIC-III and on both NLL and OOD AUROC on SST-2; many improvements have overlapping confidence intervals (acknowledged in Appendix H.1). The 'up to 33× fewer parameters than a 5-member Deep Ensemble' comparison is a weak selling point since any single-model method trivially uses fewer parameters than a 5-member ensemble.

Some presentation issues: the title and abstract oversell the singularity observation; large parts of the appendix reprove well-known results (EYM theorem, Lipschitz/smoothness of standard losses, Glorot/He initialization) at textbook length, inflating the paper's apparent theoretical content.
No code release is mentioned despite the 'from scratch' implementation and the reproducibility-focused presentation.
